newsitem.title: USA: Milwaukee stadium bonds may get MBIA insurance.
newsitem.headline: Milwaukee stadium bonds may get MBIA insurance.

text.p: An upcoming restructuring of $146.7 million of convertible option bonds into long-term, fixed-rate debt for a new Milwaukee Brewers baseball stadium will probably carry insurance from MBIA Insurance Corp, the financial adviser for the deal said Monday.

Patrick Born, a senior vice president at Evensen Dodge Inc, said the Southeast Wisconsin Professional Baseball Park District board, a state-created entity overseeing the $250 million stadium project, received proposals from three bond insurers last week and is expected to select MBIA.
"We got very good proposals," Born said.

He added that all the insurers had questions about a still-pending lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of a 0.1 percent, five-county sales tax that will be used to pay off the restructured bonds.

Born said he believed the insurers were "reasonably satisfied" the lawsuit was not going to be an issue in the future in view of a no-merit opinion on the case from the baseball park district's litigator.

The lawsuit, filed by a group of Milwaukee area taxpayers, is pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals in Chicago after a U.S. District Court judge in Milwaukee last year dismissed the case on the basis that the constitutionality of the tax had been upheld by the Wisconsin Supreme Court.
George Watts, the lead plaintiff in the case, said his group disagreed with the district's lawyer's no-merit opinion on the case and is confident the appeals court will rule in the taxpayers' favor.

While the baseball park district board had eyed pricing the restructuring next week, Born said further work on project costs and draw schedules would push the sale to the last week in February or the first week in March.
Once the bonds are priced by Bear, Stearns & Co, the senior manager, Born said a tender notice would be sent out to the owners of the convertible option bonds the board sold Dec 3.

Those bonds were sold with a mandatory tender anytime between March 1 and Dec 15. The deal, which was rated MIG-1 by Moody's Investors Service, placed the proceeds in a guarenteed investment contract provided by AAA-rated Bayerische Landesbank pending the tender.

The structure of that deal allowed the board to circumvent plans by the Milwaukee area taxpayers to file a second lawsuit challenging the bond sale. It also positioned the district to avoid potential problems with the reintroduction of a bill by U.S. Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, D-N.Y., that would prohibit the use of tax-exempt debt for professional sports stadiums.
